source: Pontis & Blandford (2016) Understanding Influence: An Empirical Test of the Data-Frame Theory of Sensemaking
finding: Rare independent test of the data-frame model on a new task type (structure tasks, not stories). All the frame activities were seen, so the model generalised in outline. But coding was hard because two or more activities often happened at once.
numbers: N=11 (6 novices with 1-5 yrs research, 5 experts with >5 yrs HCI), 4 tasks (identify and predict leaders in HCI and chemistry), think-aloud plus interviews, coded into activity chains.
quote: it has not been extensively tested with a range of sensemaking tasks
limits: Tiny sample, one lab, qualitative coding by two coders, no outcome accuracy measured. Tests fit of the vocabulary, not whether the theory predicts better results.
agent_relevance: The activities can be logged as labels, but they overlap. Our agent should make each activity a separate program-checked step so labels are not ambiguous.

source: Pontis & Blandford (2016) Understanding Influence: An Empirical Test of the Data-Frame Theory of Sensemaking
finding: The model missed activities that people actually did: judging data relevance, analysing data, and making decisions. The authors added cycles of analysis and decision-making to the model.
numbers: Seen in the 11 participants across 4 tasks; no frequencies reported in the text I read.
limits: Extension is proposed from the same data, not tested on new data.
agent_relevance: A frame loop needs an explicit step for relevance filtering and for commit/decide, not only for frame change.

source: Pontis & Blandford (2016) Understanding Influence: An Empirical Test of the Data-Frame Theory of Sensemaking
finding: Expertise moderator. Experts relied on prior knowledge (soft evidence), ran longer journeys with more turning points, and questioned source trust. Novices preselected more candidates, did surface exploration, had fewer returns and often no questioning.
numbers: 5 experts vs 6 novices; 4 tasks. Same five indicator types used by both groups; some novices used simpler frames with fewer indicators.
limits: Descriptive. No effect sizes. Experts had domain knowledge, so expertise and task knowledge are mixed.
agent_relevance: The cheap shallow path (few questioning steps) is the novice pattern. A scaffold should force the questioning step on a failed check, since the model will skip it by default.

source: Pontis & Blandford (2016) Understanding Influence: An Empirical Test of the Data-Frame Theory of Sensemaking
finding: Boundary condition. The model says people elaborate a frame until an explanation fits. In structure tasks there were several valid instantiations, so people stopped, kept, or dropped candidates after a short reflection. Some chose not to preserve a candidate that did not meet all indicators and sought a new one.
numbers: Examples from chains of participants N6 and E2; 11 participants.
limits: Qualitative.
agent_relevance: Single-answer stop rules (G3) differ from multi-solution tasks. Preserve vs drop must be decided by a checked indicator list, not by feel.

source: Klein, Jalaeian, Hoffman, Mueller (2023) The plausibility transition model for sensemaking
finding: The Klein group's own update of data-frame theory. It keeps framing, questioning and elaborating, and adds plausibility judgment at every step of a story. Reframing is described as seeking a new frame once the effort of explaining away anomalies grows too large.
numbers: Built from 23 cases (a convenience subset of 73 cases from Klein et al. 2021), judged by a single reviewer (the senior author). Literature search gave 1,042 articles, 22 kept.
quote: the initial diagnosis is wrong, the anomalies will persist and increase
limits: Hypothesis-and-theory paper. One coder, no inter-rater check, cases chosen by convenience, no hold-out test. Not an experiment.
agent_relevance: Gives a countable trigger for reframing: number and effort of anomalies explained away. We can count these in code instead of asking the model.

source: Klein, Jalaeian, Hoffman, Mueller (2023) The plausibility transition model for sensemaking
finding: Rival or neighbouring accounts of surprise and stopping. Surprise as estimated effort to explain (Foster and Keane 2015), vs surprise as prediction failure (Reisenzein 2019). Stopping rule: deepen the story until plausibility feels sufficient. This links to the illusion of explanatory depth, so stopping may be too early.
numbers: No new data. Cites Rozenblit and Keil 2002.
limits: The authors say retrieval and integration difficulty might fully explain the strain they model, so the story-building account may add nothing. Not decided.
agent_relevance: If plausibility is felt ease, a model's fluent text may feel plausible by default. Do not use model-felt plausibility as the stop rule; use external checks.

source: Klein, Jalaeian, Hoffman, Mueller (2023) The plausibility transition model for sensemaking
finding: The authors name snap-back (Cohen et al. 1997) and cognitive strain as the point where people lose faith in a story. Strain comes from more anomalies, or more effort to explain them away. Ways to reduce strain: gather more data, doubt the anomalous data, make assumptions, or expand the story.
numbers: Illustrated on Air France 447; no counts.
limits: Case illustration only.
agent_relevance: Three of the four strain-reducers are the preserve activity. Only a checked anomaly count separates healthy elaboration from fixation.

source: Dhami, Belton, De Werd, Hadzhieva, Wicke (2024) Effects of task structure and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation
finding: Study 1: how evidence is laid out changed bias. Hypotheses in rows gave less confirmation-bias strategy. The ACH-style matrix (hypotheses in columns) and plain text did not.
numbers: N=161 students. Chose the confirming hypothesis in Task 1: HypCol 61.8% (34), HypRow 39.2% (20), HypText 67.3% (37); chi2(2)=9.43, p=.009, phi=.24. Post hoc: HypRow p=.003.
limits: Students, mostly female (90.1%), age ~20; one task design; not preregistered. Outcome is one hypothesis choice.
agent_relevance: Presentation format of evidence versus hypotheses is a cheap lever. For our agent, laying each piece of evidence against every candidate frame in code is a format change, not a judged step.

source: Dhami, Belton, De Werd, Hadzhieva, Wicke (2024) Effects of task structure and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation
finding: Study 2: real analysts mostly did not show confirmation bias. Judgment coherence and cognitive reflection did not separate better from worse performers.
numbers: N=62 Dutch military analysts: 66.1% balanced strategy, 19.4% confirming, 14.5% inconsistent. 83.3% sensitive to evidence credibility. CRT mean 2.32 (SD 0.92). 91.9% non-additive; CRT vs deviation from additivity r=-0.12, p=.374.
limits: Small sample; strategy inferred from choices in two tasks. Self-selected Dutch military analysts.
agent_relevance: Warns against assuming the preserve failure is universal; it is task and format dependent. Measure it on our own logs.

source: Dhami, Belton, De Werd, Hadzhieva, Wicke (2024) Effects of task structure and confirmation bias in alternative hypotheses evaluation
finding: Reports from this paper's literature review (second-hand, not read at source): in a randomised trial of 50 analysts, ACH training did not reduce bias, 80% of the control group built an ACH-style matrix anyway, ACH users were less internally consistent and not more accurate (Dhami et al. 2019; Mandel et al. 2018). In a legal trial (Maegherman 2020, N=191) the ACH group and a bias-information control did not differ.
numbers: N=50 analysts; N=191 law students; as quoted by Dhami et al. 2024.
limits: Second-hand via the 2024 paper.
agent_relevance: Structured compare-hypotheses procedures do not help by themselves. Matches our rule that the model must not run the comparison unchecked.

source: Karvetski & Mandel (2020) Coherence of probability judgments from uncertain evidence: Does ACH help?
finding: Large null result for a frame-comparison technique. ACH users were no more coherent than a no-technique group; both showed subadditivity, unreliability and overly conservative judgments. ACH users also weighted non-diagnostic evidence as if it were diagnostic.
numbers: N=227 Canadian degree holders (Qualtrics panel), mean age 40.7, 26.4% male, between-subjects ACH vs control, six cases. ANOVA on uncertainty terms: method F=0.002, p=.85.
quote: The findings do not support the claim that ACH is effective at improving probabilistic judgment.
limits: Online non-analyst sample; ACH via a software tool; coherence tests, not accuracy against truth.
agent_relevance: Do not build a compare-frames step that only asks the model to score hypotheses. Pseudo-diagnostic weighting is a known failure of such tables.

source: Karvetski & Mandel (2020) Coherence of probability judgments from uncertain evidence: Does ACH help?
finding: The paper's own review: an earlier ACH study (Lehner et al.) found projection error did not differ with ACH training, but had only 24 participants in four conditions, so is of questionable replicability. Mandel et al. (2018) found ACH raised subadditivity.
numbers: Lehner: N=24 in 4 conditions.
limits: Second-hand for Lehner and Mandel 2018.
agent_relevance: The evidence base for comparison-style debiasing is thin and mostly null. Treat compare as unproven until tested on our agent.

source: Costa Filho, Moura, Brandao, Schmidt, Mamede (2019) Effects of deliberate reflection on diagnostic accuracy, confidence and diagnostic calibration in dermatology
finding: A prompted question-the-first-diagnosis step raised accuracy after an initial answer. It did not change confidence or calibration.
numbers: N=61 (33 reflection, 28 control), 12 images. Final accuracy 49.7% vs 38.4%, t(59)=3.33, p=.002, d=0.84. Initial accuracy 45.96 vs 40.48, p=.10, d=0.42. Confidence 64.3 vs 58.9, p=.21. Calibration p=.19. Gain in accuracy: 3.79 vs 2.08 points, p=.02.
limits: Quasi-experiment (systematic allocation, not random); final-year students not experts; reflection group was higher at baseline (d=0.42). Reflection took extra time.
agent_relevance: Supports question after a first frame is formed, but it was always applied, not signal-gated. Closest to our revise step, but fixed reflection did not repair overconfidence.

source: Costa Filho, Moura, Brandao, Schmidt, Mamede (2019) Effects of deliberate reflection on diagnostic accuracy, confidence and diagnostic calibration in dermatology
finding: Case difficulty moderator. Reflection helped on easier cases and had a smaller, non-significant effect on hard cases. Students could not predict their own performance.
numbers: Easier cases: 76.8% vs 60.1% accuracy, p=.004. Harder cases: 22.7% vs 16.7%, p=.080. Self-estimate vs actual: RG r=0.05, CG r=0.285 (ns). Calibration worse on hard cases, F(1,59)=192.15, eta2=.75.
limits: Post hoc split by difficulty.
agent_relevance: When the right frame is not in the model's repertoire, reflection alone cannot create it. A reframe needs a source of new frames (seek a frame), not only a re-look.

source: Mamede et al. (2010) Effect of availability bias and reflective reasoning on diagnostic accuracy among internal medicine residents, JAMA
finding: Search snippet only. Recent similar cases lowered second-year residents' accuracy; reflective reasoning removed that deficit.
numbers: N=36 residents (18 first-year, 18 second-year); similar-case items 1.55 vs 2.19 for others, p=.03; reflection raised scores to 2.03 (2nd year) and 2.31 (1st year), p=.006.
limits: Snippet only, small N. Read the original before relying on it.
agent_relevance: Shows a prior-case frame can mislead (preserve by availability), and a forced second look can repair it.

source: Chinn & Brewer (1993) The role of anomalous data in knowledge acquisition, Review of Educational Research 63(1)
finding: Search snippet only. Seven forms of response to anomalous data; only one accepts the data and changes the theory. The other six protect the old theory.
numbers: No numbers seen.
limits: Page returned 403 to me. Taxonomy only as described in a snippet; I did not verify the names of the seven.
agent_relevance: A ready coding scheme for preserve in our logs: label each response to a failed check as a protect type or as a theory change.

source: Alavi Naeini et al. (2023) Large Language Models are Fixated by Red Herrings: Only Connect Wall dataset
finding: A frame-misleading distractor test for LLMs. Removing red herrings, by rebuilding walls from groups drawn from different walls, raised GPT-4 solved walls from 6 to 59 and correct groups from 239 to 595 of 1,976. Models fall into the wrong group frame.
numbers: Original OCW test set GPT-4 0-shot: 6 solved walls, 239 correct groups; OCW-Randomized: 59 and 595. GPT-3.5 0-shot 0 and 114 vs 5 and 274. Human: 285/494 walls, 1405/1976 groups. 10-shot GPT-4 did not beat 0-shot.
limits: Quiz-show puzzles; walls with distractors are also harder for non-fixation reasons; 2023 models; GPT-4 still below humans even without red herrings.
agent_relevance: Direct evidence that an LLM's first strong frame misleads it. More examples did not help (1 to 10 shot), so reframing needs a structural move, not more demonstrations.

source: Kim et al. (2025) Limitations of Large Language Models in Clinical Problem-Solving Arising from Inflexible Reasoning (M-ARC)
finding: Items built so that the familiar pattern gives a wrong answer. Most LLMs did worse than physicians, several near or below chance. They were also overconfident.
numbers: 100 items. Physicians (n=5) mean 66% (SE 5.3%). Best models: Gemini-1.5-Pro 50%, o1 48%. Most models under 50%, several under 20%.
limits: Items written by the authors; only 5 physicians; early-2025 models; chain-of-thought prompts.
agent_relevance: A usable fixation benchmark where the first-recognised frame is the wrong one.

source: Shidara et al. (2026) Advances in LLM Reasoning Enable Flexibility in Clinical Problem-Solving
finding: A rival result to the above: strong reasoning models now match physicians on the same fixation benchmark. The fixation weakness was a model-generation effect, not fixed.
numbers: mARC 100 items, 15 runs per model. Best model Claude 4.1 Opus 0.751 (95% CI 0.738-0.763) vs physicians 0.66 (95% CI 0.55-0.75). On items physicians mostly missed (20/100): humans 36% vs 73% on the rest; top model decisively correct on 55.0%, wrong on 25.0%.
limits: Same authors' benchmark; items are public so contamination is possible; non-reasoning models still poor.
agent_relevance: Do not assume a fixed fixation rate. Re-measure on the model we use. Strong reasoners may need less reframe scaffolding on easy traps.

source: Huang et al. (2024) Large Language Models Cannot Self-Correct Reasoning Yet (ICLR 2024)
finding: Gains from self-correction came from knowing the right answer. Without oracle labels, asking the model to re-examine its answer did not help and often hurt.
numbers: With oracle: GPT-3.5 GSM8K 75.9 to 84.3; GPT-4 95.5 to 97.5. Intrinsic: GPT-3.5 CommonSenseQA 75.8 to 38.1 (round 1) and 41.8 (round 2); GPT-4 GSM8K 95.5 to 91.5 and 89.0.
limits: 2023 GPT-3.5/GPT-4; three benchmarks; prompts later argued by others to be sub-optimal.
agent_relevance: Strongest backing for G2 and G3. A question step needs real failing output; human reflection results (d=0.84) do not transfer unchanged to a model reflecting on its own answer.

source: Jhaveri et al. (2026) Failing to Falsify: Evaluating and Mitigating Confirmation Bias in Language Models
finding: LLMs tested on the Wason rule-discovery task confirm more than they falsify. A counter-example instruction raised rule discovery, and the higher the falsifying-to-confirming ratio, the higher the success.
numbers: 11 LLMs; success 6% to 78% with 45-turn cap; counter-example prompting raised discovery from 42% to 56% on average; distilling it generalised to the Blicket task; judge agreed with human audit 98.5% to 99.5% on 200 items per setting.
limits: Interventions shifted exploration in thinking but not non-thinking models in one figure. Toy rule-discovery task. Preprint.
agent_relevance: Supports a test-the-opposite move when a frame is held, but the effect depended on model type. Combine with a count of compatible vs incompatible tests, computed in code.

source: Kraishan (2026) The Long Road to the Same Answer: Cognitive Bias Under Escalating Reasoning Budgets
finding: More thinking tokens did not reduce bias. A one-line instruction to restate the anchor lowered anchoring more than extra thinking did, but not significantly.
numbers: 30 vignettes, 6 biases, 4 model families, 12,350 calls; reasoning vs sibling delta=+0.031, t(29)=1.45, p=.157; anchoring only bias in human direction, d=1.89; restate-the-anchor effect p=.057 on 5 items.
limits: Five items per bias; effect not significant; preprint.
agent_relevance: Dose of thinking is not a reframe. A targeted prompt that names the frame being held is a better candidate than longer reasoning.

source: Zheng, Miller, Bialkowski, Soyer, Janda (2025) Supporting Data-Frame Dynamics in AI-assisted Decision Making
finding: A design proposal using data-frame theory for human-AI decision support, with a skin cancer prototype using a concept bottleneck model. No experiment reported in the text.
numbers: None.
limits: Workshop paper, prototype only. Not evidence of benefit.
agent_relevance: Shows how frames can be stored as an explicit hypothesis plus concept scores that can be edited. An implementation pattern, not a result.

source: Pontis & Blandford (2015) exploratory study, as reported in a search snippet
finding: Snippet only. Ill-defined or missing starting frames led to arbitrary decisions and lower confidence.
numbers: 11 think-aloud sessions.
limits: Snippet only.
agent_relevance: A missing initial frame is a failure mode on its own; our S1 restate step should force a stated starting frame.

source: Sieck, Klein, Peluso, Smith, Harris-Thompson (2007) FOCUS: A Model of Sensemaking, ARI technical report
finding: Could not open (the server returned an HTML page, not the PDF). Snippet says the concept appears supported by the data, with no figures seen.
numbers: None seen.
limits: Not read. Do not cite results from it.
agent_relevance: Gap: the one in-house Klein test is unread. Needs a manual download.

source: Whitesmith (2019/2020) ACH and confirmation bias, as summarised in a search result
finding: Snippet only. ACH did not reduce confirmation bias or serial-position effects.
numbers: None seen.
limits: Second-hand.
agent_relevance: Adds to the null record for comparison-style debiasing; verify before citing.
